balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

principalOcf.title: Principal operating cash flow
principalOcf.content:
Principal operating cash flow is HKEX's own disclosed cash-flow measure, which strips out the movements in clearing-participant margin deposits and clearing-house funds that pass through the statutory operating cash flow line. Those balances belong to participants, not HKEX, and can swing the statutory OCF figure by billions between periods with no bearing on the underlying business.

For Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited: use this line, not statutory OCF, to judge cash conversion of the core exchange business; the gap between the two lines is close to the scale of participant balance movements in that period.

What to watch:

  • Principal OCF tracking core revenue and EBITDA over time
  • Large statutory-vs-principal gaps in periods of market stress (participant margin spikes)

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited: the statutory figure blends core trading/clearing/listing fees with investment income on participant margin money -- see the Core Revenue vs Gross Investment Income chart below before reading growth here as purely operational.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

revenueMix.title: Core revenue vs gross investment income
revenueMix.content:
Core revenue is HKEX's trading, clearing and listing fee income -- the business driven by market turnover and new listings. Gross investment income is earned on cash balances held for clearing participants (margin and clearing-house funds), shown before the interest rebates paid back to participants.

For Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited: investment income is a function of interest rates and the size of participant balances, not trading activity -- it roughly 8x'd from HK$1.35bn (FY2021, near-zero rates) to HK$10.97bn (FY2023, post rate-hike cycle) with no matching move in market turnover. Reading statutory revenue growth without separating the two overstates how much of HKEX's growth is coming from its franchise versus the rate cycle.

What to watch:

  • Core revenue growth in isolation as the read on market activity and listings pipeline
  • Investment income direction as a read on HKD/HIBOR rates, not the business
  • A rate-cutting cycle compressing investment income even if core revenue keeps growing

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
